extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy; economists and general educated readers interested in theory of wages and capital
extracted.subtask_description: Critical theoretical analysis of the relation between wages, labor, and capital, arguing that wages are produced by labor and not advanced from capital. The text uses historical, legal, and empirical examples to refute common economic assumptions about capital as the source of wages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wages as the produce of labor
rubrics_metrics.description: Wages include all the earnings of labor, whether taken directly by the laborer in the results of his labor or received from an employer; in either case wages are really drawn from the product of the labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives multiple illustrations (self-employing laborers, share-tenancy, metayer system, salesmen paid by percentage, whaling 'lays', Farallone egg-gatherers, sealers paid in parts of seals) to show that wages in kind or their money-equivalent are the product of the labor for which they are paid. The author insists this is a universal truth to be the starting point of analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of wages in kind and wages in money
rubrics_metrics.description: Wages paid in kind (the things the labor produces) are equivalent to wages paid in money; money in such cases is simply the equivalent of the produced goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: whalers paid a 'lay' receive oil and bone; Farallone egg-gatherers could be paid in eggs or in coin obtained from selling the eggs; a sealer switches from coin to seal parts valued by Chinese laborers. 'The money is but the equivalent of the real wages, the oil and bone.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Labor always precedes wages
rubrics_metrics.description: Payment of wages always implies the previous rendering of labor; reward is conditioned upon exertion and the labor creating value comes before the payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even with fixed wages the employer usually receives value from the labor before paying wages (weekly payroll examples). Legal exceptions (e.g., admiralty law maxim 'freight is the mother of wages') confirm that disasters preventing earning of value can also prevent wages being claimable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wages are not (generally) drawn from capital
rubrics_metrics.description: The broad assertion that wages are drawn from capital is at least largely untrue; at most only some wages (those received from an employer in some senses) might be said to be drawn from capital, but this is a restricted and misleading view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author argues that because labor creates the value from which wages are paid, there is no advance or temporary lessening of employer's capital when wages are paid; detailed inventory thought-experiment (manufacturer Monday to Saturday) demonstrates that increased finished products compensate for money paid in wages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation of value is continuous through every stage of production
rubrics_metrics.description: Value is added at each stage of a production process (ploughing, sowing, milling, spinning, ship-building stages, etc.), so partially completed products already embody value before final completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: picks vs steamship keel-plates; pig iron vs finished goods; growing crops, orchards, vineyards, animals increasing in value. Therefore wages paid during multi-stage production are matched by creation of value and do not represent an advance of capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment of wages exchanges capital of one form for another
rubrics_metrics.description: When an employer pays wages, he exchanges one form of capital (money) for another (the value created by labor, embodied in partially or fully produced goods); thus paying wages does not lessen capital but changes its form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broker analogy: exchanging silver for gold is analogous to an employer taking value created by labor (goods) and paying out money—no net advance of capital. Inventories before and after production illustrate substitution of forms of wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital is required for accumulation and exchange, not to advance wages
rubrics_metrics.description: Capital is needed when producers wish to accumulate a stock of products or to sell on credit (i.e., to place produce into the general current of exchanges without immediate re-exchange), but not for the mere payment of wages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases requiring 'capital' (e.g., building tunnels, deep mining, stocking goods) show capital is needed to hold accumulated produce or facilitate certain business forms; this capital is for accumulation/merchant/speculator functions rather than to advance wages to laborers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confounding money with wealth leads to fallacies
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimating capital by money leads to confusion; thinking 'money paid out in wages lessens capital' ignores that money is only one form of wealth and that produced goods may replace money as capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns that the 'fruitful source of economic obscurities' is treating wealth as synonymous with money. Examples: difficulty converting produced goods to money can make an employer appear to have 'exhausted' capital, though overall wealth form has changed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of capital depends on the possessor's purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles of wealth are capital only so long as they are held for exchange/production and cease to be capital when passed to those who will consume them; thus food/clothing become non-capital when intended for consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: breakfast on a laborer's table is not capital even if the same goods would be capital in another context; John Stuart Mill's attempt to remand definition 'to the mind of the possessor' is criticized as insufficient without this distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed wages vs contingent wages: risk allocation affects wage level
rubrics_metrics.description: When wages are fixed the employer takes more risk and provides assurance; fixed wages are 'always somewhat less than wages contingent' because employers are compensated for bearing risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps explain why fixed-wage laborers often have legal claims and why employers are described as taking on risk; still, on average labor producing more than wages allows employers profit—so fixed pay doesn't imply advance from capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal maxim and exceptions corroborate production-based wages
rubrics_metrics.description: Admiralty law's maxim 'freight is the mother of wages' and legal exemptions (e.g., seaman's wages contingent on earning freight) illustrate that wages depend on production/earning rather than on a prior capital advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as legal confirmation that when production fails (no freight) wages may not be claimable, thereby reinforcing the principle that production (not capital) is the source of wages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-employing and share-based labor demonstrate wages derive from labor directly
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems where laborers take earnings directly (self-employment, share-tenancy, metayer systems, saer-and-daer) show wages are plainly the product of labor without employer-supplied capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author points to historical and contemporary forms (e.g., farming in U.S., share-tenancy, Jacob working for Laban, various civilized countries' tenancy) to argue that many laborers receive their earnings directly and thus wages come from labor's produce.
